articles.title: Section 21 Eviction Notices
articles.summary: Understanding no-fault evictions, notice periods, and validity requirements under current UK legislation.

sections.heading: What is a Section 21 notice?
sections.body: A Section 21 notice is a 'no-fault' eviction — your landlord does not need to prove you've done anything wrong. It is the most common route for landlords to regain possession of their property at the end of an assured shorthold tenancy (AST). The landlord must follow strict legal procedures. If they don't, the notice is invalid and you cannot be evicted.

sections.heading: Current notice period
sections.body: Under the Housing Act 1988 (as amended), landlords must give at least 2 months' notice. For periodic tenancies, the notice must align with rental periods. The notice must be on Form 6A (prescribed form). If your landlord uses a different form or no form at all, the notice is invalid.

sections.heading: Validity requirements
sections.body: For a Section 21 notice to be valid, your landlord must have: (1) protected your deposit in a government-approved scheme within 30 days and provided prescribed information, (2) given you a valid Gas Safety Certificate before you moved in and annually thereafter, (3) provided an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) rated E or above, (4) given you the current 'How to Rent' guide, and (5) not served the notice within the first 4 months of your tenancy. If any of these are missing, the notice is invalid.

sections.heading: What to do if you receive one
sections.body: Do not panic — a Section 21 notice is only the start of a process. Check validity immediately. If the notice is invalid, inform your landlord in writing. They must issue a corrected notice and the clock restarts. If valid, you have until the notice expiry date to find new accommodation. The landlord cannot force you out without a court possession order, which takes several more weeks.

articles.title: Section 8 Eviction Grounds
articles.summary: Understanding fault-based evictions, mandatory vs discretionary grounds, and the court possession process.

sections.heading: What is a Section 8 notice?
sections.body: A Section 8 notice is served when the landlord claims you have breached the tenancy agreement. There are 17 grounds for possession under Schedule 2 of the Housing Act 1988. Grounds 1-8 are 'mandatory' — if proven, the court must grant possession. Grounds 9-17 are 'discretionary' — the court decides if eviction is reasonable.

sections.heading: Most common grounds
sections.body: Ground 8 (rent arrears): At least 2 months' rent unpaid at the time of notice AND at the time of the hearing. This is the most common mandatory ground. Ground 10 (some rent arrears): Any amount unpaid — discretionary. Ground 12 (breach of tenancy): Any breach other than rent — discretionary. Ground 14 (anti-social behaviour): Covers nuisance, harassment, and criminal behaviour. Can be mandatory or discretionary depending on severity.

sections.heading: Notice periods by ground
sections.body: Ground 8 (2 months' arrears): 2 weeks. Grounds 10-11 (rent arrears): 2 weeks. Ground 14 (ASB): Immediate — proceedings can start the day notice is served. Other grounds: 2 weeks. The court hearing typically takes 4-8 weeks from application.

sections.heading: Defending a Section 8 claim
sections.body: Attend the hearing — if you don't, the court will almost certainly grant possession. Dispute the arrears amount with bank statements. If you've made partial payments, the 2-month threshold for Ground 8 may not be met. For discretionary grounds, present evidence of your circumstances. The court can grant a suspended possession order or allow you to stay with a repayment plan.

articles.title: Deposit Protection & Disputes
articles.summary: How your deposit must be protected, the three government schemes, and how to challenge unfair deductions.

sections.heading: Your deposit must be protected
sections.body: By law, your landlord or letting agent must protect your deposit in one of three government-authorised schemes within 30 days of receiving it: TDS (Tenancy Deposit Scheme), MyDeposits, or DPS (Deposit Protection Service). They must also provide you with 'prescribed information' about the protection. If they fail to do either, you can claim compensation of 1-3x the deposit amount.

sections.heading: The three schemes compared
sections.body: DPS (Deposit Protection Service): Free for landlords, custodial scheme — DPS holds the money. TDS (Tenancy Deposit Scheme): Insured scheme — landlord holds deposit, pays insurance premium. MyDeposits: Insured scheme, similar to TDS. All three have free dispute resolution services — you don't need a solicitor to use them.

sections.heading: How to dispute deductions
sections.body: 1. Request an itemised list of proposed deductions in writing. 2. Compare against your check-in inventory and check-out report. 3. Dispute within the scheme's deadline (typically 14-30 days). 4. Upload evidence: dated photographs, correspondence, receipts. 5. An independent adjudicator reviews both sides and issues a binding decision within 28 days. The burden of proof is on the landlord.

sections.heading: Common unfair deductions
sections.body: Fair wear and tear cannot be deducted — faded paint, worn carpets, and minor scuffs are expected. Professional cleaning charges: only deductible if the property was professionally cleaned at check-in (proven by receipt) and is returned in a worse state. Replacement costs: landlord can only claim the depreciated value, not full replacement cost. Gardening: seasonal overgrowth is not a deduction.

articles.title: Landlord Repair Obligations
articles.summary: What your landlord must repair under Section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, and how to enforce your rights.

sections.heading: Section 11 — what's covered
sections.body: Under Section 11 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, your landlord must keep in repair: the structure and exterior of the property (roof, walls, windows, doors), basins, sinks, baths and sanitary installations, heating and hot water installations, and gas, electricity and water systems. This applies regardless of what the tenancy agreement says — the obligation cannot be contracted out.

sections.heading: What's not covered
sections.body: Landlords are not responsible for damage caused by the tenant, decoration (unless damage makes it necessary), appliances (unless supplied as part of the tenancy), or garden maintenance (unless specified in the agreement). The property must be fit for human habitation under the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018.

sections.heading: How to report disrepair
sections.body: 1. Report in writing (email or letter) with photographs and dates. 2. Give the landlord reasonable time to respond — typically 14 days for non-urgent repairs. 3. If ignored, contact your local council's Environmental Health department. They can inspect and serve an improvement notice requiring repairs within a set timeframe. 4. As a last resort, you can arrange repairs yourself and deduct from rent — but follow strict legal procedure or risk eviction for rent arrears.

articles.title: Rent Increase Rules
articles.summary: When and how your landlord can raise the rent, Section 13 notices, and your right to challenge at tribunal.

sections.heading: When can rent be increased?
sections.body: During a fixed-term tenancy: only if the tenancy agreement contains a rent review clause specifying when and how increases happen. Without a clause, the landlord cannot raise rent until the fixed term ends. For periodic tenancies: the landlord can increase rent once every 12 months, but must use the correct procedure.

sections.heading: The Section 13 process
sections.body: For periodic tenancies without a review clause, the landlord must serve a Section 13 notice on Form 4. The notice must give at least 1 month's notice for a monthly tenancy (or the rental period for longer periods). The proposed increase takes effect from the date stated on the form unless you challenge it.

sections.heading: Challenging an increase
sections.body: If you believe the increase is above market rate, you can refer it to the First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) before the proposed start date. The tribunal compares against market rents for similar properties in the area and sets a fair rent. You continue paying your existing rent until the tribunal decides. There is no fee to apply.

articles.title: HMO Licensing
articles.summary: What Houses in Multiple Occupation are, mandatory and additional licensing schemes, and how to check your property.

sections.heading: What is an HMO?
sections.body: A House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) is a property rented to 3 or more people forming more than one household who share facilities (kitchen, bathroom). A 'household' is a single person or members of the same family. Three unrelated professionals sharing a flat is an HMO; a couple and their friend is also an HMO.

sections.heading: Mandatory licensing
sections.body: Mandatory HMO licensing applies to properties occupied by 5 or more people forming 2+ households, over 3 or more storeys. The landlord must apply to the local council, pay a fee, and meet minimum standards for room sizes, fire safety, and amenities. Operating an unlicensed mandatory HMO is a criminal offence — landlords can face unlimited fines and rent repayment orders.

sections.heading: Additional and selective licensing
sections.body: Many London boroughs operate additional licensing schemes covering smaller HMOs (3+ people) or selective licensing covering all private rented properties in specific wards. Check your local council's website. If your landlord is unlicensed when they should be, you can apply for a Rent Repayment Order recovering up to 12 months' rent.
